solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

annotation.surface: A child's secret: the family knows that Dad keeps a weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive is part of the wordplay, and the break between dad's and weapon falls in a different place from the break in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a password is the secret word or phrase that grants access.

entries.clue: Delights Head of Planning with rental agreements (7)

indicatorNotes.Head of: the head of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A council's head of planning is thrilled with some new rental deals.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on Planning makes it look like a department title, but only its first letter counts.
annotation.definitionFit: To please someone is to delight them; both are third-person verbs.

entries.clue: Having left river, otters returned for fight (3-2)

indicatorNotes.Having left: the river letter has gone away from the word
indicatorNotes.returned: sent back the way it came, so read right to left

blocks.note: R = river, removed from OTTERS to leave OTTES

annotation.surface: Otters leave the river and come back to have a scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: R for river is a standard map abbreviation. A set-to is a brief, heated fight or argument.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: set-to is informal for a brief scrap or heated quarrel.

indicatorNotes.in: E is placed among the other letters
indicatorNotes.fancy: fancy as in elaborate or fanciful: the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: An elderly European dressed up in elaborate pyjamas.
annotation.walkthrough: Ageing reads as an adjective describing the European, but it is the definition, used in the sense of wearing down over time.
annotation.definitionFit: Weathering is ageing by exposure, as stone or wood ages outdoors.

indicatorNotes.eating: the umpire takes the pie inside

blocks.note: pork pie is rhyming slang for lie

annotation.surface: A substitute umpire tucks into a pork pie during the match.
annotation.walkthrough: Pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for lie (often shortened to porky). A relief is a replacement who takes over a shift.
annotation.definitionFit: A relief is a person who stands in for another, like a relief driver.

blocks.note: to gas is to chatter idly

annotation.surface: Instructions for someone panting and whispering.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Talk quietly' reads as one instruction, but it splits into GAS (chatter) and P, the musical mark for soft.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a gasp is a sharp, laboured intake of breath.

indicatorNotes.badly: the letters are put together badly, out of order

annotation.surface: A missionary about to fall badly from grace.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a preacher's moral failing, which is exactly the opposite of an apostle.
annotation.definitionFit: An apostle is a missionary, originally one of those sent out to spread the Christian gospel.

indicatorNotes.losing heart: the heart of GUY is its middle letter U, which goes

annotation.surface: A chubby, lovely man who is feeling discouraged.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a sweet is also the dessert course, and pud is the informal word for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Pudgy means plump or slightly fat.

indicatorNotes.unsettled: the letters are disturbed from their order

annotation.surface: Using the camp toilets upset someone's stomach.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points at an upset stomach, so 'unsettled insides' feels like one phrase; the definition is only 'insides'.
annotation.definitionFit: Entrails are the internal organs, the insides of a body.

indicatorNotes.receding: going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

annotation.surface: A hopeful headline: the climate disaster is going away.
annotation.walkthrough: Climate reads as weather, but here it is the prevailing feeling, as in the political climate.
annotation.definitionFit: Climate in its figurative sense, as in 'the climate of opinion', is the prevailing feeling of a group.

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: the letters come out in an unlucky order

annotation.surface: The better shops on the high street are sadly shutting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Closing down' looks like shops ceasing trade, but it means silencing speech or publications.
annotation.definitionFit: Censorship is the closing down of what may be said or published.

indicatorNotes.Start to: the start of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: Beginning to display a reluctant laziness.
annotation.walkthrough: LOTH is the older spelling of loath, meaning reluctant.
annotation.definitionFit: Sloth is laziness or sluggishness, one of the seven deadly sins.

entries.clue: Time to cut celery, wonky or straight (7)

indicatorNotes.to cut: T goes into the letters like a knife
indicatorNotes.wonky: crooked, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A kitchen moment: time to chop the celery, crooked or straight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wonky or straight' looks like a pair of opposites, but wonky is the anagram signal and straight alone is the definition, used as an adverb.
annotation.definitionFit: An adverb for an adverb: standing straight means standing upright, with the back held vertical.

indicatorNotes.Endless: each word loses its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone sick of never-ending, weary ridicule.
annotation.walkthrough: One 'Endless' serves both words that follow it.
annotation.definitionFit: Satire is mockery used to expose folly.

entries.clue: Dance tango with pet pig, standing up (3-4)

indicatorNotes.standing up: in a down clue, standing up means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: Tango is T in the NATO alphabet
a sow is a female pig
reversal indicator, suited to a down clue

annotation.surface: Someone dancing a tango with their pet pig, which is up on its hind legs.
annotation.walkthrough: Tango looks like the dance, but it is only the letter T; the dance is 'Dance' itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the two-step is one particular dance, a simple ballroom or country step.

entries.clue: Respect energy and power, we hear (6)

indicatorNotes.we hear: we hear it spoken rather than see it written

blocks.note: steam = power, as in full steam ahead
the two pieces run together when spoken

annotation.surface: Admiration for someone's energy and strength, according to rumour.
annotation.walkthrough: E STEAM said quickly gives ESTEEM. Energy and power look like near-synonyms, but they are two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to hold someone in high regard is to respect them.

indicatorNotes.barking: barking mad, so the letters are scrambled

annotation.surface: A male mutt barking for a longer time.
annotation.walkthrough: Barking belongs so naturally to a dog that it hides its crossword job; in British slang barking means mad.
annotation.definitionFit: A mutt is a mongrel, a dog of mixed breed.

indicatorNotes.Extremely: only the extremes, the first and last letters, are used
indicatorNotes.almost: not quite all of the word: the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: DANTE, the Italian poet, without his last letter

annotation.surface: A literary critic praising a very exact poet who is nearly a purist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely precise' reads as very exact, which is itself close to the answer's meaning; here it only supplies P and E.
annotation.definitionFit: A pedant is a purist who insists on exact rules and details.

entries.clue: Cheese boxes have something for dessert (7)

indicatorNotes.boxes: the cheese encloses the other word, as a box would

annotation.surface: A cheese board comes with something sweet to follow.
annotation.walkthrough: Boxes looks like the noun, packaging for cheese, but it is the verb: BRIE boxes OWN.
annotation.definitionFit: A brownie is a chocolate cake square often served for dessert.

indicatorNotes.Audibly: judged by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: boos are jeers of disapproval; the plural S is said as a Z

annotation.surface: Someone loudly condemns drinking.
annotation.walkthrough: BOOS said aloud is BOOZE. The surface is a temperance speaker, which makes the drink feel like the target rather than the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: booze is slang for alcoholic drink.

entries.clue: Factor in insurer underwriting show again (5)

indicatorNotes.Factor in: the answer is factored into the letters of the next words

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of insurer and the start of underwriting

annotation.surface: An insurer backing a repeat broadcast has to include it in the costs.
annotation.walkthrough: The five letters run insu-RER UN-derwriting. 'Factor in' sounds like accounting language to go with insurer and underwriting, but it points to letters sitting inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a programme broadcast a second time is shown again.

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used

annotation.surface: A fool rants about some ancient old stuff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'on the subject of', but it turns the hidden letters round.
annotation.definitionFit: A fossil, like a relic, is something surviving from the distant past.

entries.clue: Chooses initially to stay after work (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the initial letters of the words that follow

annotation.surface: Someone decides from the outset to stay late at the office.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as working overtime; 'after' is positional, putting the initials behind the work.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to opt is to make a choice between alternatives.

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: revolving, so the word turns round

blocks.note: a character in a play is a role

annotation.surface: A single composer who was a radical figure.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjective while the answer is a noun, which works because bachelor can stand before a noun, as in bachelor flat.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun defined by its key trait: a bachelor is a man who has never married, and the word works as an adjective in 'bachelor uncle'.
annotation.definitionNote: Unmarried is an adjective; BACHELOR is a noun, used here attributively.

indicatorNotes.cases of: the case of a word is its outside, the first and last letters

annotation.surface: A detective notices blatant lying in a courtroom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cases' suits the court setting, but here it means the outer shells of the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly literary: to espy something is to catch sight of it.

indicatorNotes.in: Y goes among the other letters
indicatorNotes.abroad: all over the place, so the letters are scattered

annotation.surface: An odd year spent living in a foreign capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital abroad' reads as a foreign city, but capital is simply the letters, and abroad means scattered.
annotation.definitionFit: The Greek prefix a- negates typical, so the word means departing from the norm.
